prime.problem: A recursive query like ‘everything reachable from here’ is computed by applying rules until nothing new appears. Done naïvely, each round re-derives every fact it already knows, so most of the work is repetition.
prime.fits: Last card of the batch and queries part. It builds on the previous card (fixpoint queries are PTIME) and on the graph-navigation card; it is the same idea as SQL's WITH RECURSIVE and relates to cs-3's BFS and Floyd–Warshall.
expect: δ: the facts new last round
delta rules for rules with several recursive atoms
the precedence graph and its SCCs
prime.goal: Evaluate a recursive query round by round with and without semi-naïve deltas, count the derivations, and write the delta rules for a non-linear rule.

attend: Why must any genuinely new fact in round i+1 use at least one fact that was new in round i?
On the 6-node chain both methods take 6 rounds. Where do naïve's extra 55 derivations come from?
For a rule with two recursive atoms, why does one atom read δ, the ones before it the new p and the ones after it the old p?
Why is a Datalog fixpoint guaranteed to arrive, and within how many facts?
When is building the full closure the wrong way to answer the question?

must: Datalog only adds facts → a round that adds nothing is the fixpoint → with n constants an arity-k predicate has at most n<sup>k</sup> facts → the loop ends in polynomially many rounds (fixpoint queries are PTIME)
A fact derivable only from old facts was already derived last round → every new fact needs at least one new input → join only δ, last round's new facts → 15 derivations for 15 facts instead of 70
Rule with several IDB atoms → one delta rule per atom, δ in that position, new p before it, old p after it → each combination of facts is joined once → 25 instead of 81 on the non-linear rule
Naïve and semi-naïve do the same rounds but naïve re-joins all of tc each time → work Θ(n³) vs n(n−1)/2 on an n-chain → the gap doubles as n doubles (4.7×, 8.7×, 16.7×, 32.7×)
elevated: With negation, evaluate one SCC of the precedence graph at a time in dependency order → a predicate is complete before anything negates it (stratification)
reference: the source's typos in the update rule (corrected on the card)
magic sets and delete-and-rederive as names

compress.prompt: Close the card. Write the two tc rules, then the round-by-round table for the 6-node chain: new facts, naïve derivations, semi-naïve derivations. Finish with the update rule p[i+1] = p[i] ∪ δ and one sentence on why joining only δ is enough.
checklist: δ = Δ − p: what's really new this round
a new fact must use a new fact, so old × old joins are wasted

retrieve.q: Explain why semi-naïve evaluation reaches the same fixpoint as naïve evaluation while skipping most joins.
answer: the rules are monotone, and every fact is kept
a combination of only old facts was already joined in an earlier round
so joining only combinations that contain a δ fact finds every new fact

retrieve.q: Walk through round 3 on the 6-node chain for both methods: what each joins, how many derivations it makes, and what's new.
answer: naïve re-runs the base rule (5) and joins all 9 known tc facts with edge (7 matches, since paths ending at 6 can't extend): 12 derivations
semi-naïve joins round 2's δ (1→3, 2→4, 3→5, 4→6) with edge: 3 derivations
both find 1→4, 2→5, 3→6 new; tc grows to 12

retrieve.q: You need one actor's Bacon number, not the whole co-star closure. Argue for BFS over semi-naïve closure, and what each costs.
answer: BFS from one start visits each reachable node once and each edge twice: Ω(V + E)
the full closure can hold up to V² facts
semi-naïve is the right baseline only when you need every derived fact

compare.q: Semi-naïve iteration vs Warshall's matrix closure for reachability: what does each loop over, what sets its cost, and on which graphs does each win?
answer: semi-naïve: rounds of joins driven by new facts; cost follows derived facts × edges (≤ V·E)
Warshall: a ‘direct’ triple loop, V³ whatever the graph (216 on 6 nodes)
semi-naïve wins on sparse graphs and arbitrary rules; Warshall on small dense graphs

compare.q: Running each round of the closure as a MapReduce job vs a Datalog engine's in-memory loop: what does each pay per round?
answer: MapReduce: a job start, a full shuffle of the joined relations, a DFS write per round
Datalog engine: an in-memory join of δ with edge
feeding only δ into each job keeps the semi-naïve saving, but not the per-round overhead

predict.q: Add the edge 6 → 1 to the chain, making a 6-cycle. Commit first: how many tc facts does the fixpoint hold now, how many rounds does it take, and does semi-naïve still make exactly one derivation per fact?
predict.answer: Every node reaches every node, itself included: 6 × 6 = 36 facts, in 7 rounds. Semi-naïve makes 6 derivations every round, 42 in total, so not one per fact: the last round's 6 derivations are re-derivations of known facts, found only to learn that δ is empty. Naïve makes 168. On a cycle, paths wrap around, so ‘new input’ doesn't guarantee ‘new output’.

apply.task: Run both methods by hand on the 4-cycle 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 1. For each round write δ, the naïve derivation count and the semi-naïve count, until the fixpoint. Then check with naive and semi_naive in code/semi-naive-datalog.py.
apply.done: 16 facts (every pair, including each node to itself) in 5 rounds; naïve makes 4 + 8 + 12 + 16 + 20 = 60 derivations, semi-naïve 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20. You can say why semi-naïve's last 4 derive nothing new.
apply.hint: Each round, every path gets one edge longer. After 4 rounds every path length 1–4 exists, so round 5 only re-derives.
